explain.say: Burn a log on a campfire, and only a small pile of ash is left. Did most of the wood just disappear? Look at the board, and you will find out where the mass really goes.

explain.say: It stays the same! Look at this reason. Atoms are never made or destroyed in a reaction. So the mass you start with equals the mass you end with. This is the law of conservation of mass. So where do you think the log went?

explain.say: Into the air as gases! Look at the left side of the board. When a reaction is open, gases like carbon dioxide escape, so the mass seems to drop. The log became ash plus invisible gases and water vapour. How could you stop the gas escaping?

explain.say: Seal it! Great thinking. Look at the right side: in a closed flask nothing escapes, and the scale reading stays exactly the same. Wow: Antoine Lavoisier showed this in France in the 1770s, with sealed containers and very careful weighing. You think like him!

faq.q: What is the law of conservation of mass?
faq.a: In a chemical reaction no atoms are created or destroyed, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
asks: What does conservation of mass mean?

faq.q: Why does a burning candle get lighter?
faq.a: The wax reacts with oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air. If you trapped those gases, the total mass would stay the same.
asks: Where does the candle wax go?

faq.q: Why can mass go up in a reaction?
faq.a: If a gas from the air joins in, the product gets heavier. Burning magnesium gains mass because oxygen from the air joins it to make magnesium oxide.
asks: Why does magnesium get heavier when it burns?

faq.q: How can you show mass is conserved?
faq.a: Do the reaction in a sealed container on a balance, for example mixing two solutions that form a solid. The reading stays the same before and after.
Antoine Lavoisier in France is famous for showing it in the late 1700s, by weighing reactions in sealed containers. Mikhail Lomonosov in Russia had similar ideas earlier.

facts: Antoine Lavoisier demonstrated conservation of mass in chemical reactions in the late 18th century.
When 24 g of magnesium burns completely, it combines with 16 g of oxygen to form 40 g of magnesium oxide.

quiz.say: 12 g of carbon burns completely with 32 g of oxygen. What mass of carbon dioxide forms?
quiz.show: 12 g of carbon burns completely with 32 g of oxygen. What mass of carbon dioxide forms?
quiz.why: 12 plus 32 is 44 grams; no mass is lost.

wrong.1: The oxygen's mass joins the product too.
wrong.2: You add the masses; you do not subtract them.

quiz.say: Marble chips fizz in acid in an open beaker, and the balance reading drops. Why?
quiz.show: Marble chips fizz in acid in an open beaker, and the balance reading drops. Why?
quiz.why: The reaction makes carbon dioxide, which bubbles out into the air.

wrong.0: Atoms are never destroyed in a chemical reaction.
wrong.1: The drop comes from the gas made by the reaction escaping.
